items.rss_description: Turning Volatility Into Value Underwriting RyanMeyer Wed, 10/14/2026 - 10:37 Amid today's heightened uncertainty, Dawn Miller, chief commercial officer at Lloyd's, explores how insurers can innovate their way to value both for themselves and for their clients. October 14, 2026 Image Paul Carroll We’re in an exceptionally volatile period, with major geopolitical and economic risks on top of climate-driven catastrophes, nuclear verdicts, and more. The International Insurance Society’s annual Global Insurance Forum in November, which you’re sponsoring and hosting at Lloyd’s, has as its theme this year: "Turning Volatility Into Value." How do we do that? Dawn Miller I'm just coming off some time at CIAB [Council of Insurance Agents and Brokers] in Colorado, and the topic that is on everyone's mind, in addition to market conditions, is how multiple perils are intersecting with global trends to create an increasingly varied and complex risk landscape, with some risks well modeled and others less so. In the past, our market would focus on certain CAT risks, certain natural perils happening in one place at one time. Now we're seeing multiple risks interact at the same time, from natural catastrophes and supply-chain disruption to inflation, geopolitical uncertainty and demographic risks. And those are just to name a few. It’s the interaction among these different risks that is adding new layers of complexity. We have innovations that allow us to model with more transparency, and we can bring in supplementary models to assess risk. That's a good thing. But it takes an enormous amount of creativity to predict the layers of complexity around us today. Paul Carroll Yes, some people who’ve written for us refer to a “polycrisis.” You mention modeling. Is that the main way insurers make sense of all these complicated connections, or is it improvements in scenario planning, or something else? Dawn Miller I believe it's multiple things. We're seeing innovations in modeling—additional data transparency being plugged into some of those core models that we've always used to look at some known perils. The perils aren't changing, but our ability to understand them is getting better, sometimes dramatically. There's also an opportunity for geopolitical assessments, economic assessments, and social demographic assessments to all play a role. The modeling itself is a bit of a Rubik's Cube with multiple facets to it. Paul Carroll Wall Street talks a lot about alpha and embraces volatility because it creates opportunities. Historically, insurers have not liked volatility. How do you change that thinking? Dawn Miller Given that Lloyd’s is guiding a marketplace, we're creating the conditions for success for the world's best risk takers to attach the risks they want to underwrite with capital. We see a mix in our marketplace. We do see investors coming in looking for some of that volatility. That’s what they like, and it fits as a diversifier into their portfolios. We see others wanting the longer-tail risk. This may not be as volatile, but they want it for their own investment reasons. Our role is to create the environment for all those different profiles to exist and to all benefit from the diversification of our marketplace. It's not an either-or—the alpha seekers or the beta seekers. It's having both in an environment where they can coexist. Paul Carroll Volatility requires agility not just for those transacting in your marketplace but for you, too. How is Lloyd's getting faster at identifying opportunities and scaling the winners as quickly as possible? Dawn Miller In March, we launched our new five-year strategy, Advance and protect. It is designed to sharpen Lloyd’s financial edge and maximize our unique capital advantage, including by creating a more efficient and flexible marketplace by making the platform more investable, clear, transparent and agile. Right now, there's some additional reporting, different ways of working, maybe some duplicated oversight here and there—things that have grown up over time for all the right intentions, but maybe as we evolve are not as pragmatic any more. All of those cause a little bit of extra cost, whether it's in time or resources, because time is money at the end of the day. So we're making things much clearer, making it much more cost-efficient, making sure we are an engine for driving new talent into the marketplace, attracting the best talent and then recycling them back out as advocates and having the marketplace stronger for their being with us. You're creating an ecosystem that is the center of attracting the world's best risk takers, the best capital together with the best brokers, best clients, the best risk. What that gives us is the ability to innovate. When we think about Lloyd's and the underpinnings of our strategy, our superpower is our capital diversification benefits. Our other superpowers are around our license structure, the framework we have for innovation, the ability to syndicate risk rapidly, our very strong financial strength ratings. Innovation, whether it is the birth of a new product, or the birth of a new structure, or how we deal with some of the extreme large-scale infrastructure, energy, supply chain, and transportation issues that we see around the world—that is going to take more than one mind to solve. And we are the marketplace for that sort of solution creation. Paul Carroll At ITL, in our little way, our mantra is: Nobody is as smart as everybody. Dawn Miller That's exactly right. Our role is to convene a marketplace, creating those conditions for success. It happened 338 years ago when people came together over a cup of coffee and said, Let's share this risk so we can get these ships across the globe. Today, the same principle of combining expertise and capital continues across the underwriting room, Lloyd’s Lab and Lloyd’s Academy. Paul Carroll I’m glad you mentioned the lab and the academy, because, as an old hand on innovation efforts, I wanted to ask how they fit into your broader innovation ecosystem. Dawn Miller Absolutely. As you know, Lloyd's Lab launched in 2018 to make sure we had a place to accelerate—not necessarily incubate, and I want to make that distinction—new risk-taking ideas or risk-servicing ideas. Over time, we've grown to have about 160 alumni. This past cohort, Cohort 17, just went through a selection process. We received 280 applications from 31 countries. Fifteen companies were invited to pitch to the market, and 10 were selected for the 10-week Accelerator program. The market plays a central role in that selection process because the Lab is designed to respond to real market needs. The focus of Cohort 17 has been in areas where the Lloyd’s market is actively seeking solutions that improve how the market operates day to day to strengthen its ability to respond to the complexity of today’s risk landscape and this can be seen through the themes: operational efficiency, new products and experimental innovation. What does that mean? They come in at all different stages of businesses and ideas. They have mentors from the marketplace. They hone, shift, and massage their product and their service. Then they exit the other end, generally about 80 to 85% of them, with either capacity for a proof of concept or a service contract or service proof of concept into the marketplace. That ranges from new products—cloud downtime, wildfire, data analytics—to a whole variety of services. They work their way through the market, with an accelerated cover holder process. Some of them, like Parsyl, started in the Lloyd’s Lab. Parsyl began by using data and technology to tackle risks in global health supply chains, then became a Syndicate-in-a-Box and now has in-principle approval to become a full syndicate. That’s the process of taking innovation, testing and proving it in the market, and ultimately giving it the opportunity to scale. They're a part of our ecosystem once they come out as alumni, and they stay within our ecosystem around the world. We continue to help by giving them opportunities to be exposed to end clients, to regulators, to investors, etc. Paul Carroll How do you expect these topics—including innovation, geopolitical risk, and emerging technologies—to be developed at the Global Insurance Forum? Dawn Miller I always look forward to the Global Insurance Forum; it's a place where market leaders and market practitioners are coming together to exchange on an equal level. We’re reflecting the trends of the times, whether that’s private credit, scaling innovation or how we move beyond the tactical. This year’s theme, “Turning volatility into value,” really captures that. It’s about moving beyond reacting to uncertainty and using better insight, specialist expertise and flexible capital to anticipate changing needs, build solutions and give customers the confidence to invest and grow. The companies that come together are from all around the world. Everybody's lens is going to have a slightly different take on how they deal with geopolitical risk or how they're dealing with supply chain or how they're dealing with credit risk or what they're facing at that exact moment. Bringing all of that together allows us to create a narrative that firmly implants how our industry is driving resilience forward. Our industry provides the oxygen for the economies around us. And I believe we allow our industry to represent itself or be represented by others in a way other than that. I wish we talked more about the outcome our industry enables: resilience. We need to explain insurance through communities, businesses and economies it enables to recover and thrive and persist. The forum also creates a great opportunity to bring some of our young leaders to the table. Their perspectives are varied and rich, and we need that diversity of thought. Paul Carroll As someone who’s covered technology innovations for decades, I confess that it was only about 15 years ago that I realized that none of that happens without insurance. Every major innovation—the personal computer, the internet, the smartphone, social media, search engines, GPS, the driverless car—comes with risks, and nobody can take those risks without some sort of protection. Dawn Miller Right. Isn't it funny? We all sort of take it for granted. If we could just reframe the conversation and talk more clearly about how insurance creates resilient communities, helping them thrive, we would give people a much better understanding of the value our industry provides. At Lloyd’s, we don’t just seek to understand risk, we take it on, bringing together expertise, capital and risk appetite to help businesses move forward. The issue couldn't be more important than it is right now, with the multiple layers of risks that surround us. Paul Carroll Thanks, Dawn. It’s always great talking with you. Dawn Miller Thank you for having me, Paul; always a pleasure. If you’re interested in attending the Global Insurance Forum, you can register here. Insurance Thought Leadership

items.title: Gen Z Drives Insurance Claims Transformation
items.original_title: Gen Z Drives Insurance Claims Transformation
items.rss_title: Gen Z Drives Insurance Claims Transformation
items.rss_description: Gen Z Drives Insurance Claims Transformation Customer Experience ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/14/2026 - 13:12 Gen Z's demand for instant digital experiences is forcing insurers to modernize claims payments or risk losing policyholders. October 15, 2026 Image As digital natives who've grown up tethered to smartphones and social media, the Gen Z population's effect on today's consumer trends is well documented . Young shoppers' demands for instant gratification in consumer transactions have ushered in an era of in-app shopping, next-day shipping, and fast, friction-free digital payment options. Gen Z's influence is extending to the insurance claims process, as well. More and more, Gen Z's preferences are pushing the industry to uplevel its claims experience – to make it faster, more convenient, more tied to mobile, and more transparent to the policyholder. InvoiceCloud's 2026 Claims Experience survey of 1,000 U.S. policyholders shows Gen Z is nearly twice as likely as the overall population to prefer a digital wallet for claims payments (13% versus 7%). Recent research shines a light on policyholders' discontent with what they identify as their biggest deal breaker: an unacceptably slow process for paying claims. The InvoiceCloud survey found that only 9% of policyholders received their claims payment within two days. Meanwhile, a quarter of respondents say it took more than a week to receive their claims payout, while an unfortunate 13% waited "several weeks" to get these urgent funds. This could cause ripple effects. In a 2022 report, " Transforming claims and underwriting with AI ", Accenture estimated that poor claims experiences could put up to $170 billion in global insurance premiums at risk through 2027. The InvoiceCloud survey shows how these risks could materialize. At least 75% of policyholders surveyed say they would consider switching carriers after a single negative claims experience. That's a high percentage in any field, but it's particularly high in personal-lines P&C, where switching providers is often easier than it is in commercial, E&S, or other specialty markets. Improving the claims process How do insurance carriers improve the claims process? Our research found that speed and transparency matter most of all to policyholders. When asked directly, 30% named a faster claims payment after approval as the single change they want most, more than any other option, while 22% preferred clearer status communication. Gen Z echoes that second point: 24% named clearer, more consistent communication about payment status as the one change they would make, on par with the 21% who named faster payment. Another issue: Many carriers have modernized inbound premium payments, but outbound disbursements still rely on paper checks and manual processing. Paper checks create fraud risk, delivery problems, and extra work for commissions and return premiums. The next generation of policyholders is demanding two changes to this payment structure. They prefer a shift to digital, and they want choices. Digital disbursement platforms can support a wide variety of options including ACH/direct deposit, debit cards, virtual cards, and digital wallets. Direct deposit to a bank account is policyholders' favorite payout, preferred by 52% of respondents, more than all other options combined. Printed checks still account for 19%, likely reflecting legacy carrier processes rather than genuine preference. The gap between generations is wide: 32% of Baby Boomers prefer a printed check, compared with just 9% of Gen Z. If slow payouts can lead to defections, digital insurance payments can operate as a retention tool. Insurance carriers can do this by ensuring this critical touchpoint becomes an easy experience end-to-end, from allowing policyholders to self-serve through digital premium payments, paperless billing, and automatic payments, to instant disbursements delivered however policyholders prefer to receive funds. Real-time digital disbursements are funds sent electronically and received quickly, without a paper check in the middle. For insurance carriers, this means agent commissions and return premiums move through digital payment processing solutions rather than the mail. More importantly, it means getting funds into policyholders' hands fast, when it matters the most. Raising expectations As younger policyholders account for a larger share of the insurance market, experiences they've grown accustomed to in other walks of life will increasingly become expectations for insurance as well. For many, this translates to being able to complete more transactions on smartphones. Digital payments enable customers to choose a payment method from their phone, receive payment notifications, track payment status, access transaction details, and receive funds directly into an eligible account or wallet. That matters most to the youngest policyholders. When asked for the easiest way to access funds in an emergency, 19% of Gen Z chose a mobile wallet, compared with 5% of Baby Boomers, while only 9% would withdraw cash at a bank, compared with 34% of Baby Boomers. Gen Z's imprint on insurance claims is becoming more pronounced. Today's policyholders want to have insurance claims processed and paid out faster. But they want more. They want the entire journey – culminating in how and when they get paid – to feel as immediate and seamless as any other digital financial transaction. Ray Walsh

items.rss_description: The Insurance Alignment Gap: Where Insurer Priorities and Customer Protection Needs Converge…and Diverge RyanMeyer Wed, 10/21/2026 - 10:47 Insurers are modernizing for efficiency, while customers seek affordability, trust, and protection. This report reveals how closing the alignment gap can create lasting value. October 21, 2026 Image Insurers are prioritizing cost reduction, profitability, modernization, and AI. Customers are looking for something different: affordability, trust, preparedness, and protection that feels relevant to the risks they face every day. This growing alignment gap matters. Modernization and AI investments deliver their full value only when customers see and feel the benefit. When insurer priorities and customer expectations drift apart, confidence erodes, and so does the opportunity to help customers build financial resilience. Based on original research with both insurers and insurance customers, this report examines where priorities align, where they diverge, and how insurers can connect business transformation to customer value. It explores three areas that matter most to building confidence and resilience: Relevance. Customers want protection that reflects their everyday risks. Learn how insurers can deliver coverage that feels meaningful and worth the cost. Personalization. Tailored products, pricing, and communications help customers feel understood and prepared. Learn how personalization supports trust. Digital engagement. Digital experiences shape how customers perceive their insurer. Learn how to use them to strengthen confidence and connection. Whether you lead strategy, product, distribution, customer experience, or technology, this report offers a research-based view of what customers expect and how your transformation priorities can meet them. items.extracted_text: There's a lot of hungry and extremely naive capacity available: Chubb CEO Greenberg - Artemis.bm There's a lot of hungry and extremely naive capacity available: Chubb CEO Greenberg - Artemis.bm There’s a lot of hungry and extremely naive capacity available: Chubb CEO Greenberg 21st October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Competitive insurance and reinsurance market conditions are spreading beyond just property risks, as there is “a lot of hungry and extremely naive capacity available,” Chubb CEO Evan Greenberg said today. Greenberg, speaking just now during Chubb’s third-quarter earnings call, explained that his company is being increasingly selective as it navigates a softening marketplace. The CEO noted that during Q3 Chubb shed some business in North American commercial and E&S lines, particularly property and financial lines. “North America commercial was down 2.7%, impacted again by large account and E&S property and financial lines, where we non-renewed certain business and purchased additional reinsurance,” Greenberg explained. Greenberg explained that the additional reinsurance has been purchased in certain areas of financial lines and in property risks. “We took advantage of opportunities to place additional reinsurance, which also gives us the opportunity to maintain presence and provide service and coverage to customers, and at the same time spread risk, and it was in those two areas,” Greenberg further explained. After the second-quarter, Greenberg had said that Chubb has been buying more reinsurance this year as it sees an opportunity to, as he termed it, “feed the hungry” in the competitive and softened market environment . The Chubb CEO’s comments today suggest that reinsurance buying has continued, while he continues to see a lot of “hungry” capital in the market. Today he explained, “In terms of pricing, the market continues to grow more competitive in commercial P&C across the globe, in particular the U.S. and London. “Beyond property, competitive market conditions are spreading to more casualty lines, where pricing in numerous areas is failing to keep pace with loss costs, which, while steady, continue to well-outpace general inflation.” Then he added that, “There is a lot of hungry and extremely naive capacity available. Our broad diversification, including a deep local presence in so many countries and lines of business, leave us relatively-well positioned in many areas of opportunity.” Greenberg also made some comments on the increasing entry of alternative capital into broader areas of insurance and reinsurance, including through casualty sidecars and third-party investors backing broker facilities. Greenberg stated, “You know, what drives cycles in insurance is supply and demand, and so sidecars, broker facilities, line-follow facilities, more MGAs with capital behind them other than professional insurance, and frankly a lot with professional insurance behind it. This is all throwing out of balance the supply relative to demand, and it’s a lot of very naive capacity. “Even even where it’s other than traditional insurance, it’s investor capital. There’s two brands of it to me. There’s one brand where they’re cleverly going to make a trade, even in casualty sidecars, and they have it arranged to pass the tail back to the carrier that’s fronting it who’s going to end up holding the trash, and they may make a turn. “On the other hand, I think a lot of that clever capital doesn’t understand the pricing versus the loss-cost environment, and I don’t think they’re going to end up making the turn that they think they might make. “But, we’ve been living in a world where the cost of of money is cheap, and there’s a lot of money looking for absolute return, not risk-adjusted. As you know, generally the world is beginning to change that way, but in the meantime, a lot of it has found its way, or a fraction of it has found its way into insurance as sort of an alternative investment asset class. items.extracted_text: Korra launches Deal Analysis to help ILS investors evaluate risk and transaction economics - Artemis.bm Korra launches Deal Analysis to help ILS investors evaluate risk and transaction economics - Artemis.bm Korra launches Deal Analysis to help ILS investors evaluate risk and transaction economics 21st October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Korra, the Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platform from Ledger Investing, has announced that it has launched Korra Deal Analysis, an application that’s expected to help market participants analyse the quantitative and qualitative aspects of casualty, non-catastrophe property, and specialty reinsurance and ILS opportunities. According to the announcement, Korra’s Deal Analysis application will enable ceding insurers, reinsurers, managing general agents (MGAs), fronting carriers, and the reinsurance brokers who represent them to structure, price, and publish formal risk and investment reports for their own marketing purposes. Most relevant to Artemis’ readers, however, is where Korra notes that the platform will allow insurance-linked securities investors and collateralized reinsurers to use the same analytical framework to evaluate reinsurance submissions on economic terms like IRR and MOIC instead of accounting metrics like combined ratio. “They can assess risk reliably by using transparent, back-tested stochastic models that answer important questions about the probability of downside scenarios,” Korra explained. Kyle Safran, Head of Data Science at Korra, commented: “Structuring and evaluating an ILS transaction requires understanding not only what losses may look like, but how they develop over time, flow through the deal structure, and affect each party’s economics. Safran continued: “Deal Analysis brings those pieces together — loss modeling, reinsurance structure, collateral requirements, capital structure, and investor returns — in a transparent modeling environment where reinsurance brokers and capital providers can test assumptions, compare alternative structures, and understand the distribution of potential outcomes. This gives teams an iterative and explainable way to price risk, structure transactions, and assess deal viability.” Additionally, Korra explained that its Deal Analysis application leverages AI technology to extract essential information and historical loss triangle data from reinsurance submissions, which the organisation asserts facilitates teams to quickly review and organise the historical experience needed for comprehensive analysis. Korra also added that historical performance may be examined through meaningful visualisation methods utilising a proprietary graphics library, and users can also gain access to the company’s extensive database of industry performance metrics to compare and blend data. “From there, teams can use that historical data to model prospective losses using a variety of methods, from traditional actuarial techniques to Korra’s modern, hierarchical Bayesian models that provide full probability distributions of future loss ratios. Korra’s Bayesian loss models are based on published, peer-reviewed methodologies, and are designed to work with the thin historical data often provided by MGAs by incorporating priors informed by industry data,” Korra further explained. The firm continued: “After modeling losses, users can test alternative transaction structures and model investors’ MOIC, and IRR. Analysis and forecasted results can then be packaged into investor-ready reports, giving teams a consistent way to communicate the assumptions, economics and potential outcomes of a transaction.” Korra also clarified that once a deal goes live, both the data and insights generated during its initial evaluation are carried forward in the platform and then made available as claims develop, thereby facilitating sustained monitoring of deal and portfolio performance alongside continuous reassessment of the transaction structure, while simultaneously enabling more strategically informed decisions regarding contract renewal. Meredith Barnes-Cook, Senior Principal at Datos Insights, said: “As alternative capital takes a larger share of reinsurance, brokers and investors need better tools to evaluate risk and transaction economics,” Platforms that bring actuarial modeling, deal structuring, and investor reporting into one environment make these transactions easier to assess, compare, and explain.” Umair Rasool, General Manager of Korra, added: “Risk originators and capital providers are ultimately looking at the same underlying risk from different perspectives, yet much of the analysis still happens through disconnected spreadsheets, static reports and manual workflows. “Deal Analysis gives both sides a more transparent and repeatable way to model risk, evaluate transaction economics and align on deal terms. items.title: Finding Value in Today's Volatility
items.original_title: Finding Value in Today's Volatility
items.rss_title: Finding Value in Today's Volatility
items.rss_description: Finding Value in Today's Volatility PaulCarroll Mon, 10/19/2026 - 20:00 I don't know about you, but I'm a bit wary when I pick up my phone first thing in the morning and check on the state of the world. There's rioting where? A convective storm or wildfire destroyed what? The war in Ukraine or Iran took what turn? Inflation was how high, or job growth how low? And the volatility is building on itself, creating what some of our authors have dubbed the "polycrisis." Economic problems lead to rioting in France, which destabilizes the Western alliance, which emboldens Putin in Ukraine, which feeds the political crisis in the U.S., which.... The insurance industry generally dislikes volatility. Insurers want a decade or two of data on a risk so they can price it properly. But how do you understand risks that appear so suddenly and can interact in such complex ways? To get a sense, I turned to Dawn Miller, the chief commercial officer at Lloyd's and CEO of Lloyd's Americas, who explained how new data sources, better models, scenario planning and just generally processing information faster can at least help. Let's have a look. Here is the full interview I did with Dawn. And here is a link to this year's Global Insurance Forum, which our sister organization the International Insurance Society is holding at Lloyd's in London on Nov. 15 and 16 on the theme, "Turning Volatility Into Value." But I'll summarize: Dawn says, " We're seeing innovations in modeling—additional data transparency being plugged into some of those core models that we've always used to look at some known perils. The perils aren't changing, but our ability to understand them is getting better, sometimes dramatically. There's also an opportunity for geopolitical assessments, economic assessments, and social demographic assessments to all play a role." She adds that some firms like at least some volatility because it creates more potential for upside and "fits as a diversifier into their portfolios. We see others wanting the longer-tail risk. This may not be as volatile, but they want it for their own investment reasons. Our role [at Lloyd's] is to create the environment for all those different profiles to exist and to all benefit from the diversification of our marketplace. It's not an either-or—the alpha seekers or the beta seekers. It's having both in an environment where they can coexist." Dawn cautions that today's environment is full of "new layers of complexity": "In the past, our market would focus on certain CAT risks, certain natural perils happening in one place at one time. Now we're seeing multiple risks interact at the same time, from natural catastrophes and supply-chain disruption to inflation, geopolitical uncertainty and demographic risks. And those are just to name a few.... I t takes an enormous amount of creativity to predict the layers of complexity around us today." But she's optimistic about the industry's ability to innovate, including through Lloyd's Lab and the Lloyd's Academy, to help the insurance industry react faster as perils develop and interact. She also sees the industry cooperating, including through the ecosystem that Lloyd's fosters: "Innovation, whether it is the birth of a new product, or the birth of a new structure, or how we deal with some of the extreme large-scale infrastructure, energy, supply chain, and transportation issues that we see around the world—that is going to take more than one mind to solve." When I wake up tomorrow morning, I'll still peek at my phone with one eye open to check on the state of the world, but all is not lost. I hope to see you in London so we can discuss the polycrisis and its many implications in person. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll New data sources, better models, scenario planning and faster processing of information can help insurers turn today's "polycrisis" into value for themselves and for customers. items.extracted_text: HCI Group expects Isaias losses to impact its reinsurance tower and tokenized securities - Artemis.bm HCI Group expects Isaias losses to impact its reinsurance tower and tokenized securities - Artemis.bm HCI Group expects Isaias losses to impact its reinsurance tower and tokenized securities 21st October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard HCI Group, Inc., the insurance holding company, has confirmed that only one of its three reinsurance towers has been impacted after receiving claims from Hurricane Isaias, while the company also expects one of its tokenized reinsurance securities to be affected by losses from the storm too. Hurricane Isaias made landfall close to Destin, Florida on October 9th, carrying Category 2 sustained winds of 105 mph and higher gusts. HCI’s exposure remains significantly Florida focused however the company continues to expand its underwriting platforms into additional states across the United States, including the Gulf Coast region. HCI said that the impacted reinsurance tower is Reinsurance Tower 3, which covers the northern region of Florida and has a $15 million retention, including participation by the company’s own captive reinsurers. The firm explained, “Anything above this number will be subject to the company’s reinsurance agreements.” In addition, Tower 3 is also shared between Homeowners Choice and two HCI-sponsored reciprocal insurance companies: Tailrow Insurance Exchange and Condo Owners Reciprocal Exchange (known as CORE). With respect to the company’s tokenized reinsurance securities, HCI stated that it expects only Token B to be impacted by losses from Hurricane Isaias. HCI Group’s HCI Re 2026 Series B token is a digital reinsurance security issued on the Solana blockchain via Cayman Islands-based reinsurance company Oxbridge Re Holdings’ subsidiary SurancePlus. Initially, the Series B token targeted an annualised investor return of approximately 133% but later shifted to 122%. Paresh Patel, HCI’s Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, commented: “Our thoughts are with everyone impacted by Hurricane Isaias. At this time, we are focused on supporting our policyholders by processing their claims as efficiently and effectively as possible.” Recently, Moody’s RMS Event Response team estimated that insurance industry losses from hurricane Isaias will range between $2.5 billion and $4.5 billion. Karen Clark & Company (KCC) also estimated the private insurance market loss from wind and storm surge associated with Isaias would be $3 billion . Additionally, Verisk also recently gave its initial industry insured loss estimate for Isaias, saying that onshore property losses from the storm could reach up to $2 billion . Euler ILS Partners, the specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, also put an initial insurance industry loss estimate for hurricane Isaias in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion . items.extracted_text: GM Targets ‘Eyes-Off’ Autonomous Driving for Pickups, SUVs Article 0 Comments General Motors plans to offer “eyes-off” autonomous driving on its highest-selling, most profitable vehicles — big pickup trucks and SUVs — as it seeks fresh revenue streams from heavy technology investments. Last year, GM said it would offer autonomous highway driving in 2028 on its pricey but light-selling Cadillac Escalade IQ, an electric SUV. On Wednesday, the automaker said it would expand the service to its pickup trucks and other large SUVs, without specifying a timeframe. Many assisted-driving systems control steering and speed in certain settings —sometimes hands-free — but require the driver to remain attentive. Those include Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) system and GM’s Super Cruise feature, which debuted about a decade ago. Only a few automakers have introduced eyes-off systems, including Mercedes-Benz MBGn.DE, with service typically limited to small geographic areas at low speeds, such as in stop-and-go traffic. Some industry executives have said eyes-off driving that exchanges control back and forth from the car to the driver raises thorny safety and liability questions, and might not interest enough car shoppers. Sterling Anderson, GM’s chief product officer who previously worked at autonomous-truck company Aurora, said GM is building “an autonomous system that operates safely on highways that actually gives you your time back.” He said GM will eventually expand the service to other roads. New Software Brain GM is developing a new software backbone for future vehicles to deliver the automated-driving system and other digital features, expecting drivers will be willing to pay for them. GM executives outlined the plans during an event in New York on Wednesday. A central computer will serve as the vehicle brain, allowing the car to receive remote updates like a smartphone. Tesla, Rivian and many Chinese automakers have jumped ahead of traditional automakers in designing the ability to beam software updates remotely to vehicles. Anderson said inside GM, he refers to the new vehicles as “robots.” “We’re thinking a lot about the ways your life can be better … because your vehicle just knows what you need before you need it,” he told Reuters. GM’s plan to transform cars into rolling, updatable computers is crucial to compete with Chinese automakers and EV-only brands such as Tesla, said Sam Abuelsamid, vice president of market research at Telemetry, an automotive research firm. If not, “they will fall even further behind the competitors.” One reason traditional automakers have struggled with software is that they have long outsourced much of that work to suppliers, car executives and analysts have said. Anderson said GM is developing its new “central compute” model in-house, giving the company more control over updates and functionality. “The world opens up when you control the software across the system in a way that it never was when various suppliers controlled” the car’s digital connections, Anderson said. Targeting Higher Profit Margins Automakers reap average profit margins of around 10% selling vehicles. Software-related services can reach 30% to 40% margins, according to analysis firm PwC. In a report last month, UBS estimated GM’s digital revenue will increase to $9.6 billion by 2036, from $3.2 billion this year. The bank called GM’s digital capabilities “an underappreciated and undervalued opportunity.” Ed Nightingale, GM’s vice president of digital products, said GM aims to offer car owners appealing features, because it can’t start “charging for something as part of the core experience that you’ve always had.” GM said it will introduce an AI assistant on the Cadillac Lyriq SUV in the coming months. items.extracted_text: Former Trident Reciprocal CEO Ordered to Pay $468K in Attorney and Arbitrator Fees Article 0 Comments Trident Reciprocal Exchange is one of the new kids on the Florida block. It was launched in 2024 as the long-distressed Florida property insurance market began to thaw following statutory changes that clamped down on spiraling claims lawsuits in the state. By this summer, the reciprocal held more than 24,000 policies, mostly homeowners’ policies. That’s a 45% increase from the year before, state data reports show. “We’re doing well,” said Trident Board Chairman Chris Johnson. But the firm’s journey has been marked by a big distraction and lots of litigation that had nothing to do with claims or coverage: Trident’s former CEO and co-founder, Maria Moller, a veteran of the Florida insurance business, was fired in early 2025. In a lawsuit , Trident Group Holdings accused Moller of a “brazen self-dealing scheme” in which she allegedly sent hundreds of thousands of dollars to an information technology company owned by her and her husband—all without Trident board knowledge or approval. That lawsuit in Seminole County is still pending. A judge has agreed to send it to arbitration. In a separate legal action, Moller sued Trident over her termination, alleging a breach of an employment agreement, and seeking compensation. That case also went to arbitration. In July, the arbitrator awarded Moller nothing . “Since Claimant’s termination was properly authorized and legally effective, Claimant has no right to recover any compensation and benefits after her termination date pursuant to the Executive Agreement. For different reasons, Claimant also has no right to recover any incentive compensation,” the arbitrator, Orlando attorney Garly Salzman, wrote in his decision. Moller (Linkedin) The big question then was whether Moller, the losing party in the case, would have to pay the other side’s attorney fees accumulated in the months-long lawsuit and arbitration. On Oct. 16, Salzman answered that, ordering Moller to pay some $337,800 in Trident attorneys’ fees plus another $127,476 in compensation and expenses for the arbitrator himself. “The award you reference relates solely to my employment arbitration, which we are challenging due to serious concerns regarding arbitrator bias and failure to disclose conflicts of interest,” Moller wrote in an email to Insurance Journal. Arbitration awards cannot often be appealed to a court. And a disqualification demand may have little chance of succeeding, attorneys said. Other legal wrangling is expected to continue for months or more. Moller, who previously was compliance officer for Florida-based Frontline Insurance and for Cabrillo Coastal General Insurance Agency, said this week that she has opened another front. She’s now asking a circuit judge in Orange County to dissolve Trident Group Holdings, the holding company for Trident Reciprocal. “That proceeding has an accelerated statutory framework, and we expect it to move forward expeditiously,” she said. The Lake Mary-based Trident insurance company has called the suit “nonsense” and noted that Moller had previously filed a similar suit in the same county. The judge has consolidated the suits. Johnson, the Trident Reciprocal chairman, has said that the whole episode is “sad” and ironic: The insurer had offered to settle with Moller early on. Now she finds herself facing hefty legal fees and more potentially costly litigation. Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.extracted_text: Plymouth Rock Sells Encharter Agency to MountainOne Article 0 Comments Plymouth Rock Assurance Co. has sold a western Massachusetts independent agency it bought more than 25 years ago. The buyer, MountainOne Insurance Agency, is owned by regional bank MountainOne Bank. The sale of Amherst-based Encharter Insurance Agency by Plymouth Rock was effective October 1, 2026. Terms were not disclosed. A fixture in the Amherst community since 1879 offering personal and commercial lines insurance, Encharter was formerly known as Blair, Cutting & Smith. As part of the acquisition, 22 Encharter insurance professionals join the MountainOne team, along with the agency’s Amherst office and satellite location in Lexington. North Adams-based MountainOne Insurance Agency provides personal and business property and casualty insurance, surety bonding, employee benefits, life and Medicare coverage. The acquisition of the agency in Amherst establishes MountainOne’s first insurance office in Hampshire County, continuing its expansion throughout the Pioneer Valley and adding to its local offices in Greenfield, Longmeadow, West Springfield, and Wilbraham, as well as communities throughout the Berkshires Since 1999 under Plymouth Rock Assurance’s ownership, Encharter maintained its independent agency model and relationships with multiple insurance carriers. Encharter will gradually transition to the MountainOne Insurance Agency name and brand. Boston-based Plymouth Rock offers auto, home, condo, renters, and umbrella insurance across the six Northeastern states of Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania. items.extracted_text: Mexico gets its first World Bank Cat DDO, to complement cat bonds and parametric insurance - Artemis.bm Mexico gets its first World Bank Cat DDO, to complement cat bonds and parametric insurance - Artemis.bm Mexico gets its first World Bank Cat DDO, to complement cat bonds and parametric insurance 22nd October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard The Government of Mexico has received its first World Bank Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option (Cat DDO), which will help the country prepare better and respond more quickly to natural disasters, while also complementing both of its IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 and IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 (Pacific) catastrophe bonds and parametric insurance protection. The World Bank Group has approved US $500 million in financing, marking the first time Mexico has accessed a Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option (Cat DDO). The credit line will strengthen the country’s ability to respond quickly to natural disasters, climate change impacts, and public health emergencies. For context, a Cat DDO is effectively a line of credit or borrowing from the World Bank, whereby if the government of the country announces an emergency situation it can then access the funding source. Many other countries utilise the Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option, however in Mexico’s case, this symbolises a further deepening of the country’s catastrophe risk financing and preparedness. The World Bank Group noted that the project was prepared with support from the Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery. The Cat DDO has a duration of three years, with the possibility of extension, and will support help support Mexico’s governments efforts in disaster risk management and climate resilience. Mexico is one of the most exposed countries to hurricanes, floods, droughts, and earthquakes, with a substantial share of the country’s population and territory exposed to these risks. The country already possesses a strong civil protection and emergency response system, and this Cat DDO will further support seeks to reinforce public policies that can further increase prevention and help reduce damage before it occurs. “Mexico has demonstrated exemplary leadership in emergency response and in the financial management of disaster risks, and today it is taking important steps to prevent and reduce risks. With this operation, the World Bank reaffirms its commitment to supporting Mexico in building a more prepared and resilient country. We are proud to support the Government of Mexico in this first Cat DDO,” commented Juan Pablo Uribe, World Bank Director for Mexico, Central America, and the Dominican Republic. “This support recognizes the Government of Mexico’s progress in reducing risks before disasters occur, in areas such as infrastructure, housing, energy, and health. These efforts can also contribute to employment and economic growth. When a flood, a hurricane, or a blackout disrupts activity, families, especially the most vulnerable, and businesses lose income and jobs,” World Bank Group said. As mentioned, the Cat DDO will provide additional financial protection that complements Mexico’s existing risk instruments such as catastrophe bonds and parametric insurance. Mexico has been utilising parametric risk transfer in both insurance and catastrophe bond formats for many years, developing a sophisticated natural disaster risk financing framework to which this Cat DDO adds another source and layer. During its 2026 renewal. Mexico’s Government finalised its main insurance protection for natural disasters and severe weather events for the coming year, doubling the size of its parametric catastrophe insurance arrangement to around US $575 million for 2026 into 2027 , which came into force in early June. Meanwhile, Mexico was most recently in the catastrophe bond market in May 2024, when it secured $420 million of parametric protection against earthquakes and Atlantic hurricanes from the capital markets through the IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 catastrophe bond transaction, and a further $175 million of parametric Pacific named storm protection through the IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 (Pacific) . A couple of recent hurricane events have brought the Mexican governments IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 (Pacific) cat bond issuance into focus but were not intense enough to activate the bonds parametric trigger. Cat bond investors intensely watched over as Hurricane Polo struck the west coast of Baja California Sur, Mexico in late September, with sustained winds of 110 mph and a minimum central pressure of 965mb. However, that level was not enough to trigger the cat bonds parametric trigger. Additionally, major hurricane Simon from earlier this month, also managed to avoid triggering Mexico’s Pacific named storm cat bond, as the hurricane’s path ended up shifting west and remained offshore from the important parametric trigger zones related to the cat bond. Furthermore, there was a near miss for the governments IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 catastrophe bond back in mid-July after a magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck just off the southern coast of Mexico. The World Bank noted that the new Cat DDO, “provides additional financial protection that complements existing risk instruments such as catastrophe bonds and parametric insurance. It works as an emergency credit line: if a disaster or health emergency occurs, the Government will be able to access resources almost immediately, without having to urgently reallocate the budget.” As a reminder, you can read all about the $420 million IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 cat bond that provides Atlantic hurricane and earthquake protection and the $175 million IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 (Pacific) named storm catastrophe bond, as well as more than 1,250 other cat bond transactions in the extensive Artemis Deal Directory . items.extracted_text: Fermat founders on notable catastrophe bond deals from 25 years in the ILS business - Artemis.bm Fermat founders on notable catastrophe bond deals from 25 years in the ILS business - Artemis.bm Fermat founders on notable catastrophe bond deals from 25 years in the ILS business 22nd October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Fermat Capital Management, the specialist catastrophe bond and insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, is celebrating its 25th birthday this year. The company has published a fantastic article listing 25 catastrophe bonds it feels were particularly notable from over its history, so we spoke with the co-founders to learn more. John Seo and Nelson Seo, co-founders and Managing Directors of Fermat Capital Management provided some insights into why these 25 catastrophe bonds were particularly meaningful investments for them, or deemed important transactions in ILS market history. You can see the full list of 25 notable cat bond deals over on the Fermat website . Fermat Capital Management was founded by John and Nelson in 2001 and ended that year with over $30 million in assets under management. Today, the company manages more than $11 billion of investments across catastrophe bonds and related insurance-linked securities and in its history, has traded over $60 billion in notional ILS in that time across roughly 17,500 primary and secondary market trades, while taking a lead investor position on more than 350 individual catastrophe bond deals. That’s quite the track-record and after their 25 years in the ILS market John and Nelson seem as energised as ever for the asset class and its future role in delivering efficient capital to transfer and protect against peak catastrophic risks, while developing attractive opportunities for investors. To begin our interview, we asked the Seo’s what made the 25 cat bond deals they selected particularly meaningful for Fermat? John explained, “These are all deals that we believe contributed to the market’s growth story. They either marked the entry of an important future sponsor or peril, had an innovative feature or application, triggered payouts that proved the market’s worth, or generated important learnings for investors and sponsors alike to take forward and create the rapidly growing and increasingly relevant market that we have today.” To which Nelson added, “Having been in this market since its early days, we’ve learned from each of these deals. If you’re in any market early and long enough, not only do you compound your returns for longer, you also compound your learning for longer. We believe compound learning is just as important as compound returns.” Out of the 25 deals key learnings for Fermat included, “That our asset class and catastrophe bonds have a lot of potential important applications for the future, but good risk transfer standards have always been, and will continue to be, key,” Nelson further stated. In terms of structure and the use-case for the risk transfer a catastrophe bond provided, the US Federal Emergency Management Agency’s entry into the market to source reinsurance for the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) is deemed a particularly notable one. “The inaugural NFIP Floodsmart Re deal in 2018 is a particular favourite. We worked behind the scenes for years, lending our expertise to Congress who laid the groundwork for the Floodsmart Re deals to come to market. We are looking forward to seeing the NFIP and U.S. federal government back in the market in the future,” John told us. The Fermat co-founders believe the market has developed a strong base, evidenced in the 25 cat bond deals they have highlighted. From this base the opportunity is there to continue expanding the use-case for cat bonds and ILS structures, to broaden the asset class and make insurance risk transfer more efficient and available, supported by the capital markets. “The ILS market is rapidly growing and broadening, now supporting multiple lines of re/insurance business and an expanding breadth of sponsors and perils,” Nelson said. “We believe the asset class has a lot more to do beyond re/insurance, and we look forward to seeing an even broader range of sponsors and applications in the years ahead: more corporates and sovereign sponsors, more deals addressing new pressing perils and critical risk management needs.” John added that, “The basic blueprints for these future deals already exist, ready to be used and improved.” Continuing to explain why these 25 landmark deals were selected, John said, “The list gives an insight into the deep foundation the market has built since its inception nearly three decades ago, a foundation based on the experience of committed sponsors and issuers, bold innovations, devastating catastrophes, and market loss events. It also reminds us that the asset class has, over time, proven itself to both sponsors and investors. This is timely, as the next 25 years will be very different to the last 25 years.” Nelson further explained, “The future market will not only be hurricanes and earthquakes, but a wider range of risks that are increasingly becoming too big for balance sheets to bear alone. For this critical moment, when our market is going to be needed more than ever, this list of deals represents a market that is ready for its next chapter.” Finally, we asked the Fermat Capital Management co-founders to reflect on their learnings and experienced over the 25 years since starting the firm. Nelson told us, “It’s difficult to imagine that it’s been 25 years, but it does make sense when thinking about all the incredible changes and developments that have happened in the catastrophe bond market and our company since we started Fermat. We are grateful to our investors, our employees, and our business relationships – many of whom have been with us for the majority of our history – and look forward to the next 25 years.” John added, “When Nelson and I founded Fermat 25 years ago, catastrophe bonds were still a young market. It has been both fascinating and gratifying to watch this market develop, participate in its expansion, and, of course, grow along with it. Today, the market includes more than 125 sponsors, something that would have been difficult to imagine in those early days. “One of the things that has kept the work interesting is that it sits at the intersection of finance, insurance, science, nature, and technology, which means you never stop learning and the work remains intellectually stimulating. More than anything, I’m proud of the people and the institution we’ve built here at Fermat.” You can access Fermat Capital Management’s article detailing the 25 landmark catastrophe bond deals over on the firm’s website . Look out for our exclusive video interview with John Seo next week, in which we discuss Fermat’s 25th anniversary milestone and his views on catastrophe bond and insurance-linked securities market development over the years. items.extracted_text: The Cost of Losing Your Cool: Tally the Losses of a Supermarket Cyberattack Article 0 Comments Insurance and Financial Implications of France ‘s Supermarket Refrigeration Cyberattack Keeping things cool is generally a good idea in the supermarket business. When a cyberattack reportedly interferes with refrigeration systems, the consequences can extend well beyond a few melted ice creams. The recent incident affecting French supermarkets raises complex questions about insurance coverage and, just as importantly, how to put a price on the resulting financial losses. What happened? In a cyberattack that exposed how vulnerable internet-connected systems can be, attackers took over the refrigeration equipment in hundreds of French supermarkets. Working through the units’ direct internet connections, the attackers manually changed the temperature settings on refrigerators belonging to several supermarket groups. Some reports suggest that the hackers were able to raise the temperature of the refrigerators remotely, and in some cases the units got up to 50°C (122°F) and even sparked fires. This is a somewhat rare example of a cyber incident causing a physical loss. To date, no ransom or other demand has been made, and no group has publicly claimed responsibility. About 350 supermarkets in France were affected. The refrigeration units ran software from the Danish company Danfoss. Many of the compromised units were past their end of life, meaning they no longer received software or security updates, or they were running outdated firmware. A similar attack hit a retailer in the Netherlands. That Dutch company also operates several U.S. grocery chains, including Stop & Shop and Giant Food. Which insurance applies: Cyber, P roperty, Both or Neither? Is this loss insured under cyber coverage or property coverage? Possibly both—or neither. Many property policies now contain cyber exclusions, some with carveouts for resulting fire damage. Spoilage of refrigerated stock is often covered only by endorsement or under equipment breakdown coverage, which may carry its own cyber-related limitations. To the extent the answer is cyber, the threshold question is whether these grocers purchased such coverage. Sources suggest that the uptake for cyber insurance in France lags the U.S. by a considerable margin, particularly for smaller businesses. Even in the U.S., small business uptake on cyber insurance is estimated in the range of 50%. Stock losses, business interruption and increased costs The most obvious consequence of a refrigeration failure is spoiled stock. Putting a value on the damage is not necessarily as straightforward as counting the contents of the freezers. This raises a host of questions: Should the stock be valued at the cost to the grocer? Should it be valued at retail price? Does it have salvage value? And how is a double recovery avoided if insurers are also paying for lost business interruption losses? Establishing business interruption losses under such circumstance could prove challenging for insureds, particularly where supermarkets have remained open while certain departments were temporarily closed or operating at reduced capacity. After all, a customer unable to buy frozen pizza might opt for a fresh one instead, visit another supermarket (possibly within the same retail group), or simply return when the freezers are back in action. Not every lost sale of frozen food necessarily translates into a euro-for-euro drop in profit. Nor can a reduction in turnover simply be multiplied by the supermarket’s accounting gross margin to arrive at the insurable loss. Depending on a policy wording, adjustments may be needed for uninsured working expenses, savings in variable costs, and differences in contribution margins between product categories. Even when the refrigeration equipment is back up and running, the financial consequences may linger. Replenishing stock, restoring product ranges and returning to normal trading can take time, while temporary refrigeration, expedited deliveries and other mitigation measures may add to the bill. Exclusions, business interruption triggers and attribution Cyber policies often exclude “physical damage and bodily injury.” Does this exclusion apply to the stock loss or the physical damage caused by resulting fires or physical damage to the equipment itself? Some cyber policies have exceptions to such exclusions that would restore coverage for “bricked” hardware rendered unusable by an attack. If that language were present here, it might respond to damage to the controllers, if not the refrigeration units themselves. Under U.S. law, depending on the state and the policy wording, this issue could implicate the efficient proximate cause doctrine and lead to questions as to whether the predominant cause of the damage was the cyberattack or the loss of cooling or an intervening fire. The affected grocers’ policies, however, are likely governed by French law, under which exclusions must be clear and limited (“formelle et limitée”) to be enforceable. This incident also raises questions as to whether the grocers’ income loss would fall within direct business interruption coverage or contingent business interruption coverage. It is not yet clear whether this was a coordinated, potentially automated attack against refrigeration controllers installed at individual stores or whether this was a breach of the manufacturer’s central software infrastructure. The former would implicate direct business interruption coverage, while the latter would be a contingent business interruption issue. Early reports cut both ways: French supermarket chain E.Leclerc has attributed the disruption to an attack on one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers, while Danfoss has pointed to outdated equipment at customer sites. For contingent business interruption, many cyber policies require a written contract between the insured and the dependent business that experienced the security breach, and some limit coverage to providers of IT services. Whether a refrigeration manufacturer qualifies may depend on whether it hosts or operates the remote monitoring platform. Presumably, these grocers had written contracts with the refrigerator manufacturers when the units were purchased. But do they now? Danfoss, the manufacturer of the affected controllers, has said that most of the affected units were legacy models that no longer receive software or security updates, and that it had long advised customers to update or replace them. Have these customers let their contracts expire? Are they simply operating the remote systems on their own without an active contract with the manufacturer? That could impact coverage if the attack vector is at the manufacturer level. Conversely, if the attackers exploited unsupported or unpatched equipment at the store level, insurers may point to policy conditions or exclusions addressing unsupported software or failure to apply available security patches. Attribution may also matter. No group has claimed responsibility, but if the attack is ultimately attributed to a state actor, insurers may invoke war or state-backed cyberattack exclusions, which Lloyd’s has required in standalone cyber policies since 2023. Separating incident losses from normal trading One of the challenges in assessing these claims will be distinguishing losses genuinely attributable to the incident from the usual ups and downs of supermarket trading. Seasonality, promotions, pricing changes and underlying sales trends can all affect turnover, whether or not the freezers are working. A forensic accounting assessment may therefore involve examining point-of-sale data, departmental margins, historical trading patterns and comparable unaffected stores to establish what the incident actually cost, rather than simply valuing lost stock or comparing projections to actuals. Subrogation and recovery a gainst third parties The story may not end with the insurance claim. If investigations establish grounds for recovery against equipment manufacturers, maintenance contractors, or technology providers, the financial consequences could extend further down the chain. The further upstream a vulnerability lies, the more businesses a future attack could affect, and the more parties could face recovery claims as a result. A broader operational technology problem While some officials are characterizing this event as an attack on France’s food supply, the attack could be part of a broader trend of hackers testing the security vulnerabilities of various operational technologies. In many businesses, operational technology (OT) may be less secure than IT systems. The risk extends well beyond supermarkets: There are documented concerns that U.S. water utilities also run critical systems on outdated software that is directly connected to the internet. These critical systems are vulnerable to the same type of remote attack and manipulation that could alter water chemistry or pressure and cause physical damage. The Bottom Line This incident raises important questions about the intersection of cyber and property risk. And it highlights the problem with operational technology being outdated and connected to the internet. When hackers can access physical equipment, the risk is more than lost data and business interruption it can impact health and safety. From the lens of insurance coverage, a clear understanding of the losses, their causes, and their financial consequences will be essential to navigating the claims and recovery process. items.extracted_text: WR Berkley CEO Shares Insights on AI Adoption During Q3 Call Article 0 Comments W.R. Berkley Corp. Chairman, President and CEO W. Robert Berkley, Jr. chose the third quarter of 2026 to enlighten analysts on the insurer’s journey parallel to society’s breakneck adoption of technological advances and its effect on the economy. “My colleagues many, many years ago recognized the importance of data and how that role was going to become ever more greater,” he said in his opening remarks during a conference call to discuss Q3 earnings. “We have been on a data journey for many, many years at this stage. And fortunately for us, we are reasonably well positioned as we see many of the technology tools that are being brought to bear, AI-related in particular. Data is the fuel that drives those engines.” Initially, artificial intelligence brought speed to the specialty insurer’s underwriting and claims, Berkley explained. W. Robert Berkley Jr. “While we are making our way well up that mountain, the next mountain that is before us is not just the benefits of speed, but the insights that we will be enjoying or further insights that we’ll be enjoying as it relates to decision-making,” he said. Insurance intake efficiency has improved “to the tune of 20%-plus.” Additionally, in claims, Berkley said more than 50% are settling for $5,000 or less, which “would invite the idea that we should be able to have a lower and lower human touch when it comes to this,” Berkley said. Related: WR Berkley Reports Q3 Net Income Decrease, Operating Income Up Berkley said he thinks many perceptions related to the application of AI impact white-collar labor, but he sees some influence on the rest of the labor force, namely with robotics. This could eventually impact the workers’ compensation line. “The labor force in this country and around the world is going to be a challenged as to how quickly we can retool people’s skill sets,” he said. “And there are certain jobs that are going to go away, not just because of AI in an office environment, but robotics can play an ever-increasing role. We’ve seen it to a certain extent in manufacturing.” In terms of AI liability exposure, Berkley said the insurer has worked “very diligently to make sure the exposure is identified, understood, controlled – and we’re getting paid for it.” The company does employ exclusionary language in policies when appropriate, he added. “We think that is our responsibility. And some people may like it, some people may not. But ultimately, that’s part of our responsibility in managing capital,” he explained. On the insurance market, as the insurer has remarked in the past, Berkley said directors & officers is “in the process of bottoming out.” Without going into detail, he added that “there are several pockets within the professional space that we find very attractive.” For some time Berkley has also expressed a dissatisfaction in the casualty, reinsurance and property environment, and he said the insurer is “waiting with bated breath, not in a happy way, to see what happens at 1/1 and what will follow. “That, in all likelihood, will prove to be a challenging time,” he said, adding that Berkley expects its reinsurance business to shrink at 10% rate. The commercial property market, Berkley said, “is going to get uglier before it gets prettier.” Opportunities lies within liability-related lines. Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: US Urges Fix for Widely Used Software After Critical Alerts Article 0 Comments The US government is working to address and stop any potential cybersecurity issues stemming from flaws in PHP, a widely used open-source software, that may impact federal agencies and American critical infrastructure, according to a White House official. The programming language, called PHP, contains two vulnerabilities which could potentially expose organizations using it in websites and software platforms to cyberattacks. The developers responsible for maintaining PHP said Wednesday they released software updates to patch the vulnerabilities, urging users to adopt those changes immediately. The US government is coordinating with technology companies to adopt the security fix, according to a White House official. PHP is one of the web’s most widely deployed technologies, underpinning millions of websites. Any vulnerability could therefore cascade through the internet’s software supply chain, potentially exposing online services to data theft, malware and breaches. Taking sites offline means attackers can’t reach and exploit the flaw while it’s being fixed. Alphabet Inc.-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a report published Wednesday that it had discovered the vulnerabilities with the help of several artificial intelligence tools. It said it had collaborated with OpenAI and the cybersecurity firm Calif on the work. Wiz’s report estimated that the PHP vulnerability affected around 70% of the internet and had existed undetected for more than a decade, but AI tools helped quickly identify a fix for them. “With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work,” it said. The US Office of the National Cyber Director was coordinating with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the National Security Agency and others to remediate the issue. Governments in Europe were taking websites offline Wednesday in response to warnings about the critical security vulnerabilities. Finland’s government said it was taking offline all public-facing internet services as a precautionary measure. Dutch national and local government websites were also taken down. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre said in an alert Wednesday that organizations should work to identify any systems running PHP, check them for malicious activity, and consider taking them offline until the vulnerabilities can be mitigated. The websites for the Dutch House of Representatives and the National Cyber Security Centre couldn’t be reached as of 5:40 p.m. local time. Dutch news agency ANP reported more than 100 municipalities, provinces and water boards were affected as they use a service provided by software firm Notubiz . Notubiz counts 254 Dutch local authorities as customers, according to its website. Notubiz did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Some universities in Germany and Austria have also pulled their sites, including the University of Vienna and the University of Freiburg. PHP is “everywhere” and quietly powers websites that run using WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento, according to the cybersecurity firm Huntress. PHP is also present “under the hood” of software, even though the software may not advertise that it is using it, Huntress said. When there is a critical vulnerability in PHP, Huntress advised in a report on Wednesday, “the number of places you have to go looking to identify vulnerable PHP versions gets very big, very fast.” Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at cybersecurity firm Cloudflare Inc., said in a post on X that his company had observed some “early attacks” attempting to exploit the vulnerabilities. In response, he said, Cloudflare had introduced protections for customers whose sites were shielded using its technology. Photo: Photo credit: Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. items.title: Back to basics: Understanding risk before buying insurance
items.original_title: Back to basics: Understanding risk before buying insurance
items.rss_title: Back to basics: Understanding risk before buying insurance
items.rss_description: Organisations should go back to basics and ensure they have an understanding of their own internal business model and attitude to risk before deciding what insurance to buy, according to management consultancy JPIC Group. “It means first understanding the internal business model of the organisation and the risks that it …
items.extracted_text: Back to basics: Understanding risk before buying insurance - Commercial Risk Organisations should go back to basics and ensure they have an understanding of their own internal business model and attitude to risk before deciding what insurance to buy, according to management consultancy JPIC Group. “It means first understanding the internal business model of the organisation and the risks that it faces, the location of the various types of risks, which risks it is prepared, and financially able to, retain, and only then determine where insurance and other forms of risk financing should sit,” said Praveen Sharma, JPIC Group. He explained that the structure of an optimal insurance programme can be influenced by internal business model, claims history (severity and frequency), and market conditions. “Limits, deductibles and focus on just premiums of the programme structures can become embedded over time without necessarily being revisited against the organisation’s current business model, risk profile and appetite, financial status and strategic objectives,” said Sharma. JPIC Group said a common danger is allowing the insurance renewal process to drive the risk financing strategy rather than the other way around. “An organisation, after understanding its internal business model, should evaluate both its risk appetite and risk tolerance,” said James Purvis, JPIC Group. “The terms are often misunderstood and often used together, but they are not interchangeable. Insurance strategy should reflect the individual organisation’s appetite and tolerance for risk.” According to JPIC Group, risk managers should be asking fundamental questions, such as: What are the organisation’s principal risks, which group entity could suffer a loss and where are they located? Which risks could materially affect its financial and operational objectives? What level of financial loss can the organisation absorb? What is the purpose of buying insurance for each exposure and what is the value of that insurance to the organisation? Where is earnings volatility acceptable, and where is it not? Which risks can be reduced or controlled operationally? Which risks could be retained and which risks should be transferred and what would be the total cost of risk including taxes for each option? Will the insurance programme respond in accordance with the organisation’s business and financial model and corporate tax strategies? Insurance programmes often contain elements that are the result of decisions made many years ago, and over time, the group structure and internal business model of an organisation may have changed so the insurance programme should not remain static while the organisation evolves around it, said Purvis. A robust review of risk appetite and insurance strategy should involve not just the risk or insurance team, but also representatives from finance, tax, operations, legal, property, technology and senior leadership, said JPIC Group. The objective is to build a shared understanding of: The organisation’s key exposures: What events could create the greatest financial, operational or reputational impact? Financial capacity: How much loss can the organisation comfortably absorb? Loss experience: Incident frequency, severity and volatility can provide valuable evidence when considering exposure to risk, financial and reputational impact and levels to which insurance may add value. Risk controls: Risk financing decisions should take account of the controls already in place. Strategic priorities: Risk financing decisions should support the wider business strategy. “Before asking what insurance to buy and why, organisations need a clear understanding of their risks, their financial capacity and their willingness to accept volatility. Only then can they make properly informed decisions about what to retain, what to control and what to transfer. The insurance buying strategy should be the outcome of the risk conversation – not the starting point,” said Sharma.
